assignment.objective: Write a 2,000–2,600 word research note that develops and defends a new mechanistic answer to this question: under a matched inference-compute budget, when should staged, retrieval-mediated question/answer communication among language-model agents outperform both independent sampling with final aggregation and an open shared transcript? Use the supplied seven-paper corpus as evidence, but do not merely survey it. Reconcile its conflicting empirical findings; formulate an explicit causal model of information diversity, social influence, retrieval, and synthesis; derive at least four discriminating predictions that separate your mechanism from plausible alternatives; identify what the existing literature cannot identify; and give a preregisterable experiment with conditions, randomization, estimands, power-analysis inputs, failure criteria, and an analysis plan. End with the strongest warranted conclusion and the observation most likely to falsify it.
assignment.rationale: These seven answers are the complete evidentiary corpus coverage demanded by D4 and contain, with file paths and ===== PDF PAGE N ===== markers, every element the research note requires: (1) the conflicting empirical poles to reconcile — Du 2023's debate-over-majority gains confounded by ~3x compute (answer:work:001-inv-du-debate, incl. its own boundary finding that no compute-matched comparison exists), Smit 2023's hyperparameter- and dataset-contingent null with the agreement-intensity sign flip (answer:work:002-inv-smit-mad-r2, linked contradicts Du), and Zhang 2025's matched-compute SC/CoT dominance plus the Heter-MAD result with the missing heterogeneous-SC control (answer:work:002-inv-zhang-when-r2); (2) the social-influence/conformity pathway from both sides — Lorenz 2011's bare-feedback diversity collapse without error reduction and Choi 2025's capability-dominated persuasion on ground-truth-free topics; (3) the formal constraints on the synthesis stage — Dung 1995 showing conflict adjudication is truth-neutral and symmetric ties are undecidable without external evidence (motivating retrieval as tie-breaker), and Shapiro 2011 showing merge rules are truth-neutral and stochastic LLM synthesis violates CRDT commutativity/idempotence conditions (grounding that consensus is not evidence of truth). No further bounded action can improve on this: the open raised questions require experiments outside the corpus, synthesis budget is exhausted per explicit runtime feedback, and the sole experiment adapter cannot bear on the research question. The note's thesis, causal model, predictions, limits, and preregistered design must be composed directly from these named answers, with the reported unresolved questions carried as the note's stated epistemic boundary per D6 and D8.

selected_packets.account: Du et al. 2023 (arXiv:2305.14325v1, 'Preprint. Under review', PDF p1) propose that multiple instances of the same LLM independently answer a query, then iteratively update their answers after seeing other agents' concatenated responses (short/long consensus prompts, Fig 3, PDF p4), converging to a shared final answer. TASKS (six, all gpt-3.5-turbo-0301, zero-shot; eval details PDF p13): reasoning — (1) Arithmetic (six random integers 0–30 in a+b*c+d-e*f; 100 tasks, PDF pp5,13), (2) GSM8K (100 problems, PDF pp5,13), (3) Chess Move Prediction (best 15th move after 14 PGN moves; Stockfish pawn score depth 20; 300 games, PDF pp5,13); factuality — (4) Biographies (new benchmark, 524 computer scientists, bullet facts vs Wikipedia ground truth scored by chatGPT yes/no/uncertain, PDF pp6,13), (5) MMLU (100 questions, PDF pp7,13), (6) Chess Move Validity (BIG-Bench chess-state tracking, PDF p7). BASELINES (PDF p5): Single Agent; Single Agent + Reflection; Multi-Agent (Majority) — majority vote over multiple agents' independent generations; debate uses identical starting prompt/model; majority baseline omitted for factuality tasks because responses aren't comparable (PDF p7). MAIN RESULTS (3 agents, 2 rounds, Table 1 PDF p6): Arithmetic 81.8±2.3 debate vs 69.0±4.6 majority, 67.0±4.7 single, 72.1±4.5 reflection; GSM8K 85.0±3.5 vs 81.0±3.9 majority, 77.0±4.2 single (reflection 75.0 hurts); Chess ΔPS 122.9±7.6 vs 102.2±6.2 majority, 91.4±10.6 single. So debate beats majority voting by ~13 points on arithmetic and ~21 pawn-score points on chess, but only ~4 points (within overlapping error bars) on GSM8K. FACTUALITY (Table 2 PDF p7): Biographies 73.8 vs 66.0 single; MMLU 71.1 vs 63.9; Chess Validity 45.2 vs 29.3; reflection underperforms single agent on MMLU (57.7). SCALING: headline config is 3 agents/2 rounds 'due to computational expense', but accuracy rises with agents (1→5, with summarization for 5+) and rounds (1→4) (Fig 10, PDF pp5,8); longer/stubborner prompts slow convergence but improve final accuracy (Fig 12, PDF p8); summarizing other agents' responses improves over concatenation (Fig 13, PDF p8); personas raise MMLU 71.1→74.2 (PDF p8); ChatGPT+Bard debate on 20 GSM8K problems: Bard 11, ChatGPT 14, debate 17 (PDF pp8-9). CONSENSUS: convergence to a single answer is not guaranteed in theory but observed empirically; agents are 'relatively agreeable', attributed to instruction tuning/RLHF (PDF p4); uncertain facts produce divergent initial answers that debate collapses to one 'more accurate, but not necessarily always factually correct' answer (Fig 9, PDF p8); confidently-held facts resist persuasion, so 'ease of persuasion' is proposed as a confidence probe (PDF p7); short prompts yield faster consensus (Fig 14, PDF p13); debate can flip all-initially-wrong populations to correct (PDF pp2,6). FAILURE MODES: debate sometimes converges to a wrong value that agents confidently affirm (PDF p10 limitations; incorrect-debate examples Figs 21-23, PDF p13); long debates cause models to attend only to recent generations (PDF p10). COMPUTE: the paper concedes debate is 'more costly, requiring multiple model instances and rounds' (PDF p2) and 'more computationally expensive' than other prompting techniques (PDF p10); it reports NO compute-matched comparison — majority voting at 3 agents costs ~3 generations vs debate's ~9 (3 initial + 6 updates), so the debate-vs-majority gap is confounded by roughly 3x inference compute (my inference from the procedure, PDF p4; the paper never quantifies tokens).
assumptions: The workspace file is arXiv v1 (23 May 2023, 'Preprint. Under review', PDF p1); numbers may differ from the ICML 2024 camera-ready, and per the benchmark constraint only this version is citable.

The majority-vote baseline is assumed to use the same number of agents (3) as debate, based on 'we run both baselines and our approach, using the identical starting prompt and language model' (PDF p5) and the shared '3 agents and two rounds' footnote in Table 1; the paper does not state the sample count for majority explicitly.
Compute accounting (9 vs 3 vs 1 generations) is derived from the described procedure, not from any cost table in the paper.
Error bars (± values) are taken as reported; the paper does not state whether they are standard errors or confidence intervals.

selected_packets.account: Lorenz, Rauhut, Schweitzer & Helbing (PNAS 2011, N=144) ran a lab experiment isolating how minimal social influence degrades collective estimation. DESIGN (PDF PAGE 2, 5, 6): 12 sessions of 12 ETH Zurich students each answered six factual estimation questions (Swiss population density, Swiss-Italian border length, Zurich immigration 2006, murders/rapes/assaults registered in Switzerland 2006), chosen to be moderately difficult (only 1.5% of runs always in the top reward band). Each question was answered in five consecutive private rounds from isolated cubicles; confidence (6-point Likert) was elicited after rounds 1 and 5 and never shared. Monetary rewards (4/2/1 points = 1.40/0.70/0.35 CHF for estimates within 10/20/40% of truth, all rounds paid) were deliberately non-competitive so others' estimates could only be used to approach truth, not to conform for gain. Three within-session information conditions, order randomized: (i) NO INFORMATION control — re-answer five times, reminded only of own last estimate; (ii) AGGREGATED INFORMATION — see the arithmetic mean of all 12 estimates from the previous round; (iii) FULL INFORMATION — see a figure of all 12 individual estimate trajectories over all previous rounds plus last-round numerical values. Per treatment: 24 groups (4 per question). THREE SIGNATURE EFFECTS: (1) Social influence effect — estimates converge and group diversity is strongly, significantly reduced (KS and F tests) WITHOUT significant reduction of collective error; effects 'almost null' in control (PDF PAGE 3, Fig 1D/E). (2) Range reduction effect — a wisdom-of-crowd indicator (centrality of the truth among sorted estimates; max 6 for n=12) declines over rounds with information exchange; regression over all questions: ~1 unit lower than control, and the decline is STRONGER under aggregated than full information, which authors link to gossip-from-fewer-sources findings (PDF PAGE 4-5). (3) Confidence effect — confidence is significantly boosted in both information conditions vs control, despite no accuracy gains: 'subjective' reliability rises as 'objective' reliability falls, a psychological trap (PDF PAGE 4 caption, PAGE 5). WHEN INFLUENCE HELPED VS UNDERMINED: it undermined in all three ways whenever questions were hard/uncertain, but there was a slight collective-error decline, especially in the aggregated condition, which the authors attribute to an artifact: right-skewed estimates make the arithmetic mean feedback higher than most estimates and above the truth, while the geometric mean of first estimates sits slightly below the truth, so mean feedback induces an upward drift toward truth — 'this effect may be different for different sets of questions' (PDF PAGE 3 footnote). Undermining was 'less severe for easier questions and if individuals are more confident' (SI Appendix, cited PDF PAGE 5). Aggregation note: arithmetic mean beat individual first estimates in only 21.3% of cases; geometric mean in 77.1% (log-transform justified by right-skew); Table 1 gives per-question aggregates (PDF PAGE 3). AUTHORS' INTERPRETATION: even bare numerical feedback — no persuasion, leaders, or strategic incentives — triggers herding; diversity loss 'appears to be a necessary byproduct of transparent decision-making processes'; convergence breeds collective overconfidence (PDF PAGE 5). CAVEATS: initial diversity was higher in control (possible anticipatory conservatism, mainly crime questions); 10 of 864x5 values removed (outliers, 'fun moves'); human students, six right-skewed estimation tasks only (PDF PAGE 3, 5-6).
assumptions: The extracted text's ===== PDF PAGE N ===== markers faithfully correspond to the printed PNAS pages 9020-9025.
Regression effect sizes quoted only graphically (Fig 2B) are accurately paraphrased by the text ('about one unit lower'; 'substantially and significantly boosted').
The SI Appendix (significance tests, moderation analysis) is outside the evidentiary corpus and therefore treated as unavailable rather than as confirming anything.

selected_packets.account: Choi et al. 2025 (ACL Findings) ran >2,500 structured LLM debates on five ground-truth-free social topics with proponent, opponent, and neutral (always GPT-4o) agents, manipulating group size (1:2, 2:1, up to 1:8) and 'intelligence' (parameter size, large vs small models from GPT/Claude/Qwen). Conformity here is evaluator persuasion on opinion topics, not accuracy change on verifiable tasks.

selected_packets.account: Dung 1995 supplies exactly the formal vocabulary for the 'synthesis competence' node: an argumentation framework AF = (AR, attacks) treats answers as abstract atoms linked by a binary attack relation, with no internal structure, weight, or truth value. Admissibility (a conflict-free set that defends every member against all attackers) is the core rationality constraint; on top of it Dung defines a lattice of semantics with different guarantees: preferred extensions (maximal admissible sets; always at least one exists, but symmetric conflicts like the Nixon diamond yield several, so credulous justification is non-unique), stable extensions (conflict-free sets attacking every outside argument; strictly stronger than preferred and may fail to exist at all), and the grounded extension (least fixed point of the characteristic function F_AF(S) = {A | A acceptable wrt S}; always unique, but can be empty — the skeptical adjudicator may justifiably endorse nothing when two agent answers attack each other symmetrically). Complete extensions bridge the two: every preferred extension is complete, and the grounded extension is the least complete one. The key coincidence result for adjudication design: well-founded frameworks (no infinite attack chains) have exactly one extension that is simultaneously grounded, preferred, and stable — the formal condition under which conflict adjudication is unambiguous. Equally important for the note: the framework deliberately does NOT model evidential weight, attack strength, truth, or probabilistic confidence — Dung himself lists differentiating attack strength as necessary future work. Consequence for the research problem: Dung-style adjudication can tell a synthesizer which set of conflicting agent answers is defensible, but it cannot break symmetric ties (two mutually attacking answers produce two preferred extensions and an empty grounded one); whatever breaks the tie — retrieval of external evidence, in our mechanism — is precisely what the formalism lacks and what retrieval-mediated Q/A supplies. claims.statement: Admissibility machinery: S is conflict-free iff no two arguments in S attack each other (Def 5, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`); A is acceptable wrt S iff every attacker of A is itself attacked by S, and a conflict-free S is admissible iff all its members are acceptable wrt S — i.e., a rational agent's accepted set must defend itself against all attacks (Def 6, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`). The Fundamental Lemma (adding an acceptable argument to an admissible set preserves admissibility) and Thm 11 (admissible sets form a complete partial order) follow (`===== PDF PAGE 7 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension of an argumentation framework AF is a maximal (with respect to set inclusion) admissible set of AF. ... This argumentation framework has two preferred extensions ... Corollary 12. Every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension.

claims.statement: Preferred extensions are maximal (w.r.t. set inclusion) admissible sets and define the credulous semantics (Def 7, `===== PDF PAGE 7 =====`). Existence is guaranteed — every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension (Cor 12) — but uniqueness is not: the Nixon diamond ({A,B}, {(A,B),(B,A)}) has exactly two preferred extensions, so under symmetric mutual attack between two agents' answers the credulous semantics licenses either conclusion and cannot choose between them (`===== PDF PAGE 7 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 13. A conflict-free set of arguments S is called a stable extension iff S attacks each argument which does not belong to S. ... Lemma 15. Every stable extension is a preferred extension but not vice versa. ... the empty set is a preferred extension of AF which is clearly not stable.

claims.statement: Stable extensions are conflict-free sets that attack every argument outside the set (Def 13, equivalently S = {A | A is not attacked by S}, Lemma 14, `===== PDF PAGE 8 =====`). Every stable extension is preferred but not conversely (Lemma 15: the self-attacking single-argument framework has the empty set as a preferred extension that is not stable), and stable extensions may fail to exist at all — Dung argues such 'anomalies' reflect the modeled world, not a bug, i.e., no adjudication guarantee is available in general (`===== PDF PAGE 8 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 20. The grounded extension of an argumentation framework AF, denoted by GE_AF, is the least fixed point of F_AF. ... Example 22 ... it follows immediately that the grounded extension is empty, i.e. a skeptical reasoner will not include anything.
Theorem 25. (1) Each preferred extension is a complete extension, but not vice versa. (2) The grounded extension is the least (with respect to set inclusion) complete extension.
Theorem 30. Every well-founded argumentation framework has exactly one complete extension which is grounded, preferred and stable.

claims.statement: Grounded (skeptical) semantics: the characteristic function F_AF(S) = {A | A acceptable wrt S} is monotonic, and the grounded extension GE is its least fixed point (Defs 16, 20, `===== PDF PAGE 9 =====`) — hence GE always exists and is unique, but may be empty: in the Nixon diamond 'a skeptical reasoner will not include anything' (Example 22). Complete extensions (admissible sets containing every argument acceptable wrt them, Def 23) link the two poles: each preferred extension is complete and GE is the least complete extension (Thm 25, `===== PDF PAGE 10 =====`). Coincidence condition: well-founded frameworks (no infinite attack sequence A_{i+1} attacks A_i) have exactly one complete extension which is simultaneously grounded, preferred, and stable (Thm 30, `===== PDF PAGE 11 =====`) — the formal condition under which adjudication of conflicting answers is unambiguous.

citations.excerpt: the idea of argumentational reasoning is that a statement is believable if it can be argued successfully against attacking arguments. In other words, whether or not a rational agent believes in a statement depends on whether or not the argument supporting this statement can be successfully defended against the counterarguments.

In general, we expect that the attacks against some arguments may have different strengths, one may be more 'deadly' than the others. So a study of how to differentiate the strength of arguments is necessary.

counterevidence: The 'does not model truth/weight' reading is an absence-of-machinery claim: the paper's Definitions 2-31 contain no weight, probability, or truth-value constructs, and the PDF PAGE 31 passage is the author's own confirmation; it cannot be proven from the text beyond this.
claims.statement: What the framework does NOT model: evidential weight, attack strength, truth, or probabilistic confidence. Justification is purely relational 'external stability' — a statement is believable iff it can be successfully defended against counterarguments (`===== PDF PAGE 3 =====`); arguments carry no internal structure or truth status (Def 2, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`); and Dung explicitly concedes that 'the attacks against some arguments may have different strengths... a study of how to differentiate the strength of arguments is necessary' and leaves it to future work (`===== PDF PAGE 31 =====`). No probability, no degrees of belief, no aggregation of independent evidential support: two arguments with identical attack graphs are treated identically regardless of the evidence behind them — so symmetric conflicts between agent answers are formally undecidable inside the framework and must be broken by information the semantics does not represent.

counterevidence: Dung does connect argumentation to logic programming, default logic, autoepistemic logic, and n-person games (Sections 3-4), so the framework is not purely syntax — but these reductions inherit the same attack-graph-only information; none adds evidential weight or truth.

The grounded extension being empty in the Nixon diamond is a feature (skeptical caution), not a defect, from Dung's perspective; using 'empty GE = adjudication failure' in the note is our task-specific interpretation, not Dung's claim.

selected_packets.account: Shapiro et al. 2011 formalize exactly the merge/aggregation stage of any multi-agent pipeline: how concurrent contributions combine without central coordination. Core machinery: (1) A Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT) is a replicated data type whose design satisfies sufficient conditions for Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC); SEC = eventual consistency (eventual delivery, convergence, termination) plus Strong Convergence — correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state immediately, with no consensus, no roll-back, and no waiting for quiescence (Defs. 2–3, page 4). (2) Two sufficient conditions: state-based CvRDT — payload forms a join semilattice, merge computes the least upper bound (commutative, idempotent, associative), and state is monotonically non-decreasing; Theorem 1 gives SEC assuming eventual delivery and termination (pages 4–5). Op-based CmRDT — updates split into a side-effect-free prepare step at the source and an effect-update delivered downstream; if all concurrent updates commute and delivery is reliable and causally ordered, Theorem 2 gives SEC (pages 5–6). (3) The two styles are mutually emulatable (Theorems 3–4, pages 7–8), so 'merge states' vs 'merge operations' is an implementation choice, not a difference in guarantee. (4) Scope and limits: SEC solves the CAP dilemma by staying available and partition-tolerant without consensus, tolerating n−1 crashes (page 6); but eventual delivery alone is insufficient (no-op merge counterexample, page 4), and SEC is incomparable with sequential consistency — the converged state need not correspond to any sequential execution (page 8). Crucially for the research note, the guarantees are truth-neutral: correctness is defined relative to a chosen concurrent specification, not relative to fact. Add-wins, remove-wins, highest-IP-wins, or reset-to-⊥ all satisfy strong convergence ('any of them may be reasonable for some application', page 8); LWW imposes a total order 'at the cost of losing concurrent updates' (page 13). Cross-paper inference for the note (not Shapiro's claim): both independent-sampling-plus-aggregation and staged Q/A must pick a merge rule for agent contributions, and CRDT theory shows that rule choice determines which contributions survive aggregation while saying nothing about whether the merged content is true — formally grounding the dossier constraint that agreement or merge success is not evidence of correctness. A further diagnostic for the note: LLM free-text synthesis is generally neither commutative nor idempotent, so it fails the CRDT sufficient conditions and inherits no convergence guarantee at all.

boundary_findings.alternative_explanation: An LLM synthesizer could be engineered to approximate idempotence (e.g., deterministic decoding over a fixed evidence union), partially restoring CRDT-like behavior; this is an empirical design question, not excluded by the paper.
boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: The note would overclaim that a merged/agreed multi-agent answer is well-defined or reliable merely because contributions were combined, conflating convergence (a structural property) with correctness — exactly the constraint the dossier forbids.

boundary_findings.narrative: CRDT guarantees presuppose deterministic, mathematically constrained merge operators (LUB or commuting operations). LLM-based answer synthesis — the actual merge stage in both focal baseline conditions — is stochastic, non-idempotent, and non-commutative, so none of Shapiro's convergence theorems apply to it directly. CRDT theory functions as a diagnostic boundary (what properties a merge must have for agreement to be well-defined), not as an applicable guarantee.

citations.excerpt: Definition 3 (Strong eventual consistency (SEC)). An object is Strongly Eventually Consistent if it is Eventually Consistent and: Strong Convergence: Correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state: ∀i,j : ci = cj ⇒ si ≡ sj.
In our conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), an update does not require synchronisation, and CRDT replicas provably converge to a correct common state.

claims.statement: Shapiro et al. define a CRDT as a data type satisfying sufficient conditions for Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC), where SEC is eventual consistency (eventual delivery, convergence, termination) plus Strong Convergence: correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state (∀i,j: ci=cj ⇒ si≡sj), without consensus or roll-back.

citations.excerpt: Theorem 1 (Convergent Replicated Data Type (CvRDT)). Assuming eventual delivery and termination, any state-based object that satisfies the monotonic semilattice property is SEC.
It follows that ⊔ is: commutative: x⊔y = y⊔x; idempotent: x⊔x = x; and associative: (x⊔y)⊔z = x⊔(y⊔z).

claims.statement: State-based sufficient condition (CvRDT, Theorem 1): if the payload forms a join semilattice under ≤, merge computes the least upper bound (LUB), and state is monotonically non-decreasing across updates, then the object is SEC assuming eventual delivery and termination. The LUB is commutative, idempotent, and associative, so state-based merge is insensitive to message order and duplication.

citations.excerpt: Theorem 2 (Commutative Replicated Data Type (CmRDT)). Assuming causal delivery of updates and method termination, any op-based object that satisfies the commutativity property for all concurrent updates, and whose delivery precondition is satisfied by causal delivery, is SEC.
An op-based object has no merge method; instead an update is split into a pair (t,u), where t is a side-effect-free prepare-update method and u is an effect-update method.

claims.statement: Operation-based sufficient condition (CmRDT, Theorem 2): an update is split into a side-effect-free prepare-update at the source replica and an effect-update delivered to all replicas; if all concurrent updates commute (Def. 6) and the delivery precondition is satisfied by reliable causally-ordered broadcast, then the object is SEC assuming termination.

citations.excerpt: Theorem 3 (CmRDT emulation). Any SEC state-based object can be emulated by a SEC op-based object of a corresponding interface.
Theorem 4 (CvRDT emulation). Any SEC op-based object can be emulated by a SEC state-based object of a corresponding interface.

claims.statement: State-based and op-based CRDTs are equivalent in expressive power: any SEC state-based object can be emulated by a SEC op-based object (Theorem 3) and vice versa (Theorem 4), so the choice between shipping state and shipping operations is an implementation matter that does not change the convergence guarantee.

citations.excerpt: SEC provides an extreme form of fault tolerance, as a SEC object tolerates up to n−1 simultaneous crashes. Remarkably, SEC does not require to solve consensus.
if the merge method m is a no-op, an update executed at some replica has no effect on other replicas, and they will never converge.
Such a state would never occur in a sequentially-consistent execution... Therefore, SEC is incomparable with sequential consistency.

claims.statement: The guarantees and their boundaries: SEC replicas remain available and converge under partitions without solving consensus, tolerating n−1 crashes (a proposed solution to CAP); but eventual delivery alone does not imply convergence (a no-op merge method never converges), and SEC is incomparable with sequential consistency — a converged SEC state may be unreachable in any sequential execution.

citations.excerpt: the add could win, or the remove could win, or the update of the replica with the highest IP address could win, or the state might be reset to a distinguished state ⊥, and so on. All these alternatives satisfy the strong convergence condition, and any of them may be reasonable for some application.
LWW ensures a total order of operations, at the cost of losing concurrent updates.
CRDTs are guaranteed to converge towards a common, correct state, without requiring any synchronisation.

counterevidence: The paper's own wording 'correct common state' (pages 2, 14) could be misread as a content-truth guarantee; the surrounding formalism defines 'correct' strictly as conformance to the data type's concurrent specification, not as factual correctness of payload content.
claims.statement: CRDT correctness is specification-relative, not truth-relative: for concurrent conflicting updates, add-wins, remove-wins, highest-IP-wins, or reset-to-⊥ all satisfy strong convergence and the paper states any of them may be reasonable for some application; LWW-style rules impose order only 'at the cost of losing concurrent updates'. Convergence and agreement therefore certify nothing about which merged content is true or even retained.

counterevidence: Shapiro et al. themselves use 'correct state' language (===== PDF PAGE 2 =====, ===== PDF PAGE 14 =====); a careless reading could cite this as evidence that CRDT-style merging certifies content correctness, whereas the paper's own add-wins/remove-wins discussion (page 8) shows correctness is spec-relative.

All guarantees are asymptotic and conditional: eventual delivery over fair-lossy channels, method termination, and (op-based) causal-order broadcast; no timing, bandwidth, or staleness bounds are provided, and remove-style operations require tombstones or unique tags (pages 9–11), so naive set-union intuitions do not cover deletion/retraction of agent claims.

Mapping CRDT merge semantics onto LLM answer aggregation is the investigator's cross-domain inference, not a claim of the paper; the paper addresses deterministic replicated data types, not stochastic model outputs.

raised_questions.acceptance_condition: For each candidate aggregation operator, a deterministic test (e.g., permuting input order, duplicating an input) establishes whether outputs are invariant (commutative/idempotent) or not, with effect sizes on final-answer variability reported for at least the operators used in the note's experiment.
discriminating_outcomes: If LLM synthesis output is invariant to input order and duplication, CRDT-style convergence reasoning transfers and merge design is not a confound.

If output varies materially under order/duplication perturbation, aggregation is a variance source that must be controlled (fixed order, averaged over seeds) in the experiment, and union/vote aggregators gain a formal advantage over synthesis aggregators.
raised_questions.rationale: Shapiro's theorems give convergence only when merge is a semilattice LUB or updates commute (pages 5–6). Both focal baselines (independent sampling + aggregation, staged Q/A) end in an aggregation step; if that step is a stochastic LLM call, it violates these conditions, so final answers may depend on agent ordering and sampling noise — a confound for the preregistered matched-compute experiment and a mechanistic distinction between aggregation designs.
raised_questions.text: Which aggregation operators used in multi-agent LLM pipelines (majority vote, evidence union, LLM free-text synthesis) satisfy or violate the CRDT sufficient conditions for well-defined merging (commutativity, idempotence, monotonicity), and does order/non-determinism of the final aggregation step measurably change the merged answer?

unresolved: Whether any aggregation operator actually used in multi-agent LLM systems (majority vote, evidence-union, LLM free-text synthesis) satisfies commutativity/idempotence/monotonicity; LLM synthesis plausibly violates all three, meaning staged Q/A and independent+aggregation pipelines may have no convergence guarantee of the CRDT kind — a diagnostic the research note should exploit but this extraction cannot settle.
The paper gives no guidance on merging weighted, probabilistic, or natural-language content; adapting semilattice machinery to confidence-bearing claims is open.

selected_packets.account: Smit et al. 2023 (ICML 2024, arXiv:2311.17371v3) benchmark three MAD protocols — Society of Mind (Du et al. 2023), Multi-Persona (Liang et al. 2023, angel/devil/judge), ChatEval's three modes (Chan et al. 2023) — against non-debate multi-call strategies (Self-Consistency, Ensemble Refinement, Medprompt without its kNN component) and Single Agent, crossed with five agent-level prompts, on seven multiple-choice datasets (MedQA 1273, PubMedQA 500, MMLU-clinical 123, CosmosQA 500, CIAR 50, GPQA 448, Chess-short 1000), primarily GPT-3.5-turbo with GPT-4/Mixtral-8x7B checks on MedQA. Cost is USD per question and average API calls per question (plus time and prompt length in appendices). Headline: with original implementations MAD does not reliably beat Self-Consistency or Medprompt (Medprompt best overall: MedQA 0.65, PubMedQA 0.77; Single Agent best on GPQA 0.33; no protocol dominates all datasets), and MAD uses more API calls/tokens/cost. A K-fold analysis (pick hyperparameters best on two held-out same-category datasets) flips the winner between medical and non-medical groups, showing optimal settings are dataset-specific and no protocol is assured to beat single-agent on new data. Debate-vs-first-answer gains are protocol-dependent: SoM gains substantially, ChatEval modestly, Multi-Persona loses accuracy because the devil agent disagrees even with correct first answers. The paper's own mechanism claim: prompting 'agreement intensity' modulates first-round agreement and accuracy, with dataset-dependent sign — high agreement helps MedQA/PubMedQA, disagreement helps counter-intuitive CIAR; tuning yields ~15% for Multi-Persona and ~5% for SoM on a 376-question USMLE subset, and 90%-agreement Multi-Persona sets a claimed GPT-3 state-of-the-art on full MedQA. Hyperparameters transfer GPT-3.5→GPT-4 but not to Mixtral-8x7B. Stated limitations: API nondeterminism/model updates; cost-limited scale.

claims.statement: SCOPE: Smit et al. benchmark three debate protocols — Society of Mind (Du et al. 2023), Multi-Persona (Liang et al. 2023; angel/devil agents plus judge that can end debate early), ChatEval in three modes (one-on-one, simultaneous-talk, simultaneous-talk-with-summarizer; Chan et al. 2023) — plus non-debate multi-call strategies Self-Consistency and Ensemble Refinement, Medprompt, and Single Agent, on seven datasets: MedQA (1273 USMLE 4-choice), PubMedQA (500), MMLU clinical topics (123), CosmosQA (500 subsampled of 7000 for cost), CIAR (50 counter-intuitive arithmetic), GPQA (448), and BIG-Bench Chess state-tracking (Short setting, 1000 games). Base model: GPT-3.5-turbo chosen for cost/performance balance; GPT-4 and Mixtral-8x7B additionally evaluated on MedQA only.

claims.statement: HEADLINE NULL/ADVERSE RESULT: 'multi-agent debating systems, in their current form, do not reliably outperform other proposed prompting strategies, such as self-consistency and ensembling using multiple reasoning paths' (Abstract). Best-configuration Table 2: no protocol dominates all datasets; Medprompt is best overall (MedQA 0.65 vs SoM/ER 0.64, ChatEval/SC/Single 0.60, Multi-Persona 0.58; PubMedQA 0.77; MMLU 0.74 vs Self-Consistency's 0.78). On the reasoning datasets 'the debating protocols do not outperform the other protocols': Single Agent is best on GPQA (0.33) and competitive on CosmosQA/CIAR; on Chess, Multi-Persona 0.33 barely exceeds Single/ER/ChatEval 0.32 while SoM 0.26 and Self-Consistency 0.27 fall below. Multi-Persona runs 'consistently about 7% worse than the Medprompt strategy', and single-agent plus self-consistency accuracy 'can be manipulated via prompts to achieve a high variance'.

Self-Consistency and Medprompt emerge as the top performers. Conversely... single-agent methods surpass all evaluated systems except for Multi-Persona and Self-Consistency.

claims.statement: K-FOLD HYPERPARAMETER SENSITIVITY: datasets are divided into medical vs non-medical groups; for each method and dataset, the hyperparameter combination with the highest average accuracy on the two held-out same-category datasets is used to compute final accuracy (Fig 3). Result: within medical datasets every evaluated system outperforms single-agent methods except Multi-Persona, with Self-Consistency and Medprompt top; within non-medical datasets single-agent surpasses all systems except Multi-Persona and Self-Consistency. Authors' conclusion: 'hyperparameter choices significantly influence system performance, with optimal settings tending to be dataset-specific... superior performance of various protocols over a standard single-agent approach is not assured for new datasets.'

the Multi-Persona system reduces the overall performance compared to relying solely on the initial response of the first agent. This can be attributed to the role of the second agent (the 'devil'), which is deliberately designed to contradict or disagree, even if the initial response was correct.

claims.statement: DEBATE-VS-FIRST-ANSWER IMPROVEMENT (Fig 4, averaged over all datasets): relative to the first agent's initial answer, ChatEval shows a modest enhancement, Society of Mind a substantial increase, and Multi-Persona a DECREASE — the debate process reduces accuracy relative to its own first answer. The authors attribute this to the devil agent being 'deliberately designed to contradict or disagree, even if the initial response was correct', concluding that agents' prior willingness to agree at the outset of a debate is a critical 'hyperparameter'.

we apply the 90% agreement intensity agent prompts to Multi-Persona on the full MedQA dataset and demonstrate (as far as we are aware) a new state-of-the-art result (for GPT-3), highlighted in Figure 1 by the red cross symbol.
hyperparameter settings can be effectively transferred to GPT-4. However, this transferability does not extend well to Mixtral 8x7B.

claims.statement: PAPER'S OWN ACCOUNT OF WHEN DEBATE HELPS — AGREEMENT MODULATION: a new prompt ('you should agree with the other agents X% of the time') modulates first-round agreement, which drives final accuracy, but the sign is dataset-dependent: MedQA and PubMedQA directly benefit from HIGH agreement while counter-intuitive CIAR follows the reverse pattern (strong disagreement raises the chance of reaching the correct answer). On a 376-question USMLE subset, sweeping agreement intensity yields ~15% accuracy improvement for Multi-Persona and ~5% for SoM, while ChatEval is 'hardly affected'; applying 90% agreement Multi-Persona to the full MedQA dataset gives a claimed new GPT-3 state-of-the-art, surpassing Medprompt and Self-Consistency (red cross, Fig 1). Tuned hyperparameters transfer GPT-3.5→GPT-4 on MedQA but not to Mixtral-8x7B, attributed to architectural differences. Spider-plot analysis (Fig 7) shows SoM has the largest surface across debating metrics (consensus accuracy, any-correct-answer, answer changes, unique first answers).

citations.excerpt: Limitations We utilize API calls to a publicly available LLM which... exposes us to variable inference time calls and unforeseen model updates... MAD approaches currently do not outperform other ensembling methods such as Medprompt and self-consistency using their original implementations. MAD typically requires a higher number of API calls... this might primarily be due to MAD protocols being more sensitive to hyperparameters.

claims.statement: STATED LIMITATIONS AND CONCLUSION FRAMING: the authors concede that reliance on a public API 'exposes us to variable inference time calls and unforeseen model updates' and that 'large-scale API-based benchmarking incurs substantial financial and time costs, which both limit the experiment scales and provide a barrier of entry to replication'; they recommend open-source models for future work. Their stated conclusion is that MAD's deficit 'might primarily be due to MAD protocols being more sensitive to hyperparameters and not necessarily that debate inherently performs worse than single-agent methods', while noting 'MAD typically requires a higher number of API calls, increasing the number of tokens to produce and process and ultimately, the total running cost of the system.'

counterevidence: The paper is not a pure null result: after agreement-intensity tuning, Multi-Persona moves from worst to best protocol and claims a GPT-3 state-of-the-art on MedQA (PDF p.6-7), so 'debate never helps' would misread it; the finding is that debate's benefit is hyperparameter- and dataset-contingent.
GPT-4 spot checks (Fig 8, PDF p.8) suggest conclusions may shift with model capability; the headline null is established mainly on GPT-3.5-turbo.

selected_packets.account: Zhang et al. 2025 (arXiv:2502.08788v3; position paper subtitled 'Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate—We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity') is the corpus's decisive matched-compute reappraisal. DESIGN: 5 MAD frameworks (SoM=Du et al. 2023, Multi-Persona, Exchange-of-Thoughts, ChatEval, AgentVerse) x 9 benchmarks (general knowledge: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, AGIEval; math: GSM8K, MATH; programming: HumanEval, MBPP) x 4 models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-haiku, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b), vs SA/CoT/SC baselines, debate rounds adjusted so every MAD method uses ~6 LLM calls; 3 repetitions with std (===== PDF PAGE 1, 6, 7 =====). HEADLINE: no MAD method exceeds a 20% win rate vs CoT across 36 scenarios; SoM/EoT/ChatEval/AgentVerse win ~15%, MP 0%; worse on programming, relatively better on math; the gap widens vs self-consistency at comparable LLM-call or token budgets (===== PDF PAGE 3, 7-8 =====). RECONCILIATION: MAD beats direct single-agent prompting in 34/45 GPT-4o-mini conditions—'perfectly aligns with previous findings'—but SoM and ChatEval were never compared to CoT in their original papers, so Du-style positives hold only against the weakest baseline (===== PDF PAGE 8 =====). HYPERPARAMETERS: agents 3->9, rounds 2->4 yield mostly stagnation or decline (sole exception EoT on GSM8K), ruling out misconfiguration as a universal explanation (===== PDF PAGE 8-9 =====). EFFICIENCY: SC converts extra tokens into accuracy; MAD is flat (SoM on MMLU) or trails SC at comparable tokens (EoT); per-question analysis shows aggressive methods (MP/ChatEval/AgentVerse) correct many errors but flip many correct answers, while conservative ones (SoM/EoT) avoid new errors but correct few—a correction/instability trade-off (===== PDF PAGE 9, 25 =====). HETEROGENEITY: Heter-MAD (each generation queries a random model from {GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-70b}, p=0.5) improves every tested framework (+6.4% SoM, +8.2% EoT vs single-model averages; up to +5.8% vs CoT-Average), with gains concentrated where models have complementary solvability and in simpler frameworks—'a universal antidote' (===== PDF PAGE 1, 4, 10-13 =====). POSITIONING: credits Du et al. 2023 as foundational but attributes MAD's overvaluation to fragmented, selective evaluation (Table 5 shows minimal benchmark overlap across prior MAD papers); aligns with Smit et al. 2024's null while dismissing its medical-only scope; flags that agents debate whole responses yet rebut final-answer differences rather than reasoning, and that current benchmarks need only single knowledge points (===== PDF PAGE 2, 5, 13, 14, 15 =====). Key identification gap for the root note: no heterogeneous self-consistency control, so the debate-specific value of heterogeneity over plain decorrelated sampling is not identified.

boundary_findings.consequence_if_absorbed: The research note would overcredit staged communication/deliberation: if mixed-model SC matches Heter-MAD at matched compute, heterogeneity evidence supports a diversity-only mechanism and undercuts any claim that debate structure itself adds value.

Heter-MAD is compared only to same-model MAD averages and CoT-Average. The communication channel's contribution beyond error decorrelation is therefore unidentified in this paper — the exact gap the root note's discriminating predictions must close.

claims.statement: Zhang et al. 2025 evaluate 5 MAD frameworks (SoM, Multi-Persona, Exchange-of-Thoughts, ChatEval, AgentVerse) x 9 benchmarks spanning general knowledge (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, AGIEval), math (GSM8K, MATH), and programming (HumanEval, MBPP) x 4 foundation models (GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-haiku, Llama3.1-8b, Llama3.1-70b), against SA/CoT/SC baselines; debate rounds are adjusted so all MAD methods align to ~6 LLM calls by default, T=1/top-p=1, win/tie/lose vs CoT decided by ANOVA with p>0.05 counted as a tie, and all experiments repeated three times with standard deviations ('===== PDF PAGE 1 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 6 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 7 =====').

citations.excerpt: none of these MAD methods achieve a win rate higher than 20% when compared to CoT across 36 scenarios (4 models × 9 benchmarks)
SoM, EoT, ChatEval, and AgentVerse only outperformed CoT in approximately 15% cases, while MP did not demonstrate significant improvement over CoT

claims.statement: Headline negative result: no MAD method achieves a win rate higher than 20% vs CoT across 36 scenarios (4 models x 9 benchmarks); SoM, EoT, ChatEval and AgentVerse outperform CoT in only ~15% of cases and MP in 0%; by task type, MAD performs worst on programming and relatively best on mathematical reasoning ('===== PDF PAGE 3 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 7 =====').

citations.excerpt: the underperformance becomes even more pronounced when compared to SC, especially when using a comparable number of LLM calls or tokens

claims.statement: The matched-compute comparison is decisive: MAD's underperformance 'becomes even more pronounced when compared to SC, especially when using a comparable number of LLM calls or tokens' — i.e., independent sampling plus majority-vote aggregation dominates debate at equal inference budget ('===== PDF PAGE 3 =====').

citations.excerpt: MAD frameworks outperform SA in most conditions (34 out of 45 conditions utilizing GPT-4o-mini), which perfectly aligns with previous findings in the field

claims.statement: Reconciliation with prior positives: MAD frameworks outperform direct single-agent prompting (SA) in 34 of 45 GPT-4o-mini conditions, 'which perfectly aligns with previous findings in the field', but ChatEval and SoM were never compared to CoT in their original papers, MP was compared to CoT only on the undisclosed CIAR dataset, EoT's CoT advantage replicates only on Claude-3.5-haiku, and AgentVerse's HumanEval edge relies on an extra execution-evaluation stage 'arguably beyond the scope of MAD designs' ('===== PDF PAGE 8 =====').

citations.excerpt: increasing the number of agents or debate rounds often results in either stagnation or even a decline in performance... rules out suboptimal hyperparameter configurations as a universal explanation

claims.statement: Hyperparameter scaling does not rescue MAD: increasing debate rounds 2->4 or agents 3->9 leaves outcomes mostly unchanged or declining (e.g., SoM still underperforms CoT on MMLU and HumanEval at 4 rounds or 9 agents); the sole exception is EoT on GSM8K, which improves continuously from 3 to 9 agents and surpasses CoT — so suboptimal hyperparameters are ruled out as a universal explanation for MAD's inferiority ('===== PDF PAGE 8 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 9 =====').

citations.excerpt: SC effectively utilizes the increased inference budget. However, MAD frameworks either: (i) show no positive trend... or (ii) continue to underperform SC while consuming a comparable number of tokens
overly aggressive methods may introduce instability, while conservative methods may struggle to capitalize on opportunities for correction

claims.statement: Efficiency and mechanism: SC 'effectively utilizes the increased inference budget' while MAD either shows no positive scaling with tokens (SoM on MMLU) or improves yet still underperforms SC at comparable token counts (EoT on MMLU/GSM8K); per-question error analysis reveals a correction/instability trade-off — MP, ChatEval and AgentVerse correct many wrong answers but also erroneously flip many initially correct ones, whereas SoM and EoT are conservative, introducing few new errors but correcting few ('===== PDF PAGE 9 =====', Figure 6 on '===== PDF PAGE 25 =====').

citations.excerpt: Heter-SoM improves SoM-average by 6.4%, and Heter-EoT improves EoT-average by 8.2%... all the considered MAD methods outperform CoT-Average by up to 5.8%
Using identical agents from the same model undermines the very premise of debate—diverse knowledge and reasoning

counterevidence: Gains are benchmarked against the AVERAGE of the two single-model MAD runs, not the best single model: e.g., on MMLU SoM-Llama (84.6) exceeds SoM-Heter (83.5), and vs CoT-Average several per-benchmark cells are negative (ARC-Challenge -1.4%, MBPP -2.0%) ('===== PDF PAGE 11 =====' Table 4) — 'universal antidote' holds on average, not per benchmark.

No heterogeneous self-consistency control (mixed-model majority vote with no communication) was run, so the debate-specific contribution of heterogeneity beyond decorrelated sampling is not identified.
claims.statement: Model heterogeneity as 'a universal antidote': Heter-MAD, where each agent generation queries a randomly drawn model from {GPT-4o-mini, Llama3.1-70b} with p=0.5, consistently improves all tested frameworks — Heter-SoM +6.4% and Heter-EoT +8.2% over the average of the two single-model runs, and all heterogeneous MAD variants beat CoT-Average by up to +5.8%; gains concentrate on questions where the two models have complementary solvability (CW/WC categories), simpler frameworks (SoM, EoT) benefit more than complex ones (ChatEval, AgentVerse), and the authors argue identical agents 'undermine the very premise of debate' ('===== PDF PAGE 1 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 4 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 10 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 11 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 12-13 =====').

citations.excerpt: Smit et al. (2024) found that MAD methods do not reliably outperform other ensembling reasoning strategies. However, they specifically focus on medical prompting methods and medical benchmarks, which limits the generalizability
rebuttals focus on outcome differences rather than analyzing the logic behind discrepancies

claims.statement: Positioning and self-identified limits: the paper credits Du et al. 2023's SoM as the foundational MAD design and replicates its MAD>SA result, but attributes MAD's overvaluation to fragmented, selective evaluation — Table 5 shows minimal benchmark overlap among prior MAD papers; it aligns with Smit et al. (2024)'s finding that MAD does not reliably outperform ensembling strategies while criticizing its medical-only scope as limiting generalizability, and notes Khan et al. 2024's single-agent comparison was calibrated and limited to three datasets; its future agenda flags that agents 'engage in debates based solely on their complete responses... rebuttals focus on outcome differences rather than analyzing the logic behind discrepancies', and that current benchmarks 'require only a single knowledge point', so scenarios needing genuinely distributed knowledge may better suit MAD ('===== PDF PAGE 2 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 5 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 13 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 14 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 15 =====').

counterevidence: The win/tie/lose classification counts ANOVA p>0.05 as a 'tie' with only 3 repetitions per condition, so the ~40-60% tie rates partly reflect low statistical power rather than proven equivalence; the direction of the effect, however, is corroborated by the raw accuracies in Table 3 (e.g., SoM below CoT on 6 of 9 GPT-4o-mini benchmarks) ('===== PDF PAGE 3 =====', '===== PDF PAGE 7 =====').

MAD does beat direct single-agent prompting in 34/45 conditions, and SoM beats CoT on GSM8K across all round variations; debate is not uniformly harmful — the negative result is specifically against CoT/SC as stronger baselines ('===== PDF PAGE 8-9 =====').

Default matching is by LLM-call count (6), but MAD prompts embed peers' full responses, inflating input tokens; the token-level efficiency comparison relies on Figure 6 (appendix), and proprietary-model token counts could not be precisely controlled ('===== PDF PAGE 9 =====').

selected_packets.objective: What does Zhang et al. 2025 (papers/text/zhang-et-al-2025-mad-question.txt, 'If Multi-Agent Debate Is the Answer, What Is the Question?') establish: the 5 MAD methods x 9 benchmarks x 4 models design; the headline negative result that MAD methods rarely beat CoT (win rates under 20% across 36 scenarios) and underperform self-consistency at comparable LLM-call/token budgets; the hyperparameter experiments (agents 3-9, rounds 2-4) showing stagnation/decline; efficiency findings on inference-budget utilization; the model-heterogeneity result as a 'universal antidote'; robustness findings; and how the paper positions itself against Du et al. 2023 and Smit et al. Keep the answer compact: at most 8 claims, each with a `===== PDF PAGE N =====` marker.

raised_questions.acceptance_condition: A matched-compute experiment crossing communication (none/SC vs SoM-style debate) x pool (homogeneous vs heterogeneous models) on >=3 task strata, reporting accuracy with CIs and a preregistered decision rule: if Heter-SC >= Heter-MAD, diversity-only is supported; if Heter-MAD > Heter-SC by a preregistered margin, communication adds identifiable value.
discriminating_outcomes: Heter-SC ≈ Heter-MAD at equal budget → communication contributes nothing beyond decorrelated sampling; staged retrieval-mediated designs must justify themselves on other grounds (e.g., token efficiency of selective exchange).
Heter-MAD > Heter-SC only on multi-knowledge/compositional tasks → deliberation value is conditioned on task topology, supporting the root note's moderator structure.
Heter-MAD > Heter-SC uniformly → a genuine deliberation effect exists and the note's mechanism must explain what communication adds beyond diversity.
raised_questions.rationale: Zhang's 'universal antidote' compares Heter-MAD only to same-model MAD averages and CoT-Average; without a heterogeneous-SC control, the heterogeneity result cannot distinguish a diversity-only mechanism (decorrelated errors suffice) from a deliberation mechanism (communication adds value given diversity). This is the pivotal discrimination for the root note's causal model and its predictions.
raised_questions.text: Under matched LLM-call and token budgets, does heterogeneous self-consistency (each sample drawn from a distinct model, majority vote, no inter-agent communication) match or exceed Heter-MAD, and does the answer interact with task type?

raised_questions.acceptance_condition: Construct or select task strata scored by number of required complementary knowledge/fact units (verified by ablating information given to single agents), then test the communication-condition x stratum interaction at matched compute with adequate power for the interaction, not just main effects.
discriminating_outcomes: Ordering flips in favor of staged/debate conditions as knowledge-requirement grows → task topology is a real moderator; the corpus null is scope-limited.
No interaction: SC dominates at all strata → the topology conjecture is falsified and the negative result generalizes.
raised_questions.rationale: Zhang's own boundary claim ('===== PDF PAGE 14 =====') is that current benchmarks need only a single knowledge point, so MAD may be unnecessary there; if true, the headline negative result is task-topology-confounded and the root note must stratify by knowledge-requirement rather than treat the null as universal.
raised_questions.text: Does the MAD-vs-SC ordering reverse on tasks that genuinely require combining multiple, distributed knowledge points, as Zhang conjectures but never tests?

unresolved: Whether heterogeneous self-consistency (mixed-model sampling + majority vote, no communication) matches Heter-MAD at matched calls/tokens — the control needed to attribute heterogeneity gains to debate rather than to error decorrelation alone.

Why aggressive MAD variants flip initially correct answers: Zhang's corrected/erred analysis is behavioral and cannot distinguish social-influence conformity (Lorenz/Choi-style) from noise amplification or judge/aggregation failures.
Whether task topology (benchmarks requiring multiple, complementary knowledge points) reverses the MAD vs SC ordering — Zhang conjectures yes ('===== PDF PAGE 14 =====') but tests nothing.

The three focal communication conditions are staged retrieval-mediated Q/A, independent sampling plus final aggregation, and an open shared transcript.

context.task: Write a 2,000–2,600 word research note that develops and defends a new mechanistic answer to this question: under a matched inference-compute budget, when should staged, retrieval-mediated question/answer communication among language-model agents outperform both independent sampling with final aggregation and an open shared transcript? Use the supplied seven-paper corpus as evidence, but do not merely survey it. Reconcile its conflicting empirical findings; formulate an explicit causal model of information diversity, social influence, retrieval, and synthesis; derive at least four discriminating predictions that separate your mechanism from plausible alternatives; identify what the existing literature cannot identify; and give a preregisterable experiment with conditions, randomization, estimands, power-analysis inputs, failure criteria, and an analysis plan. End with the strongest warranted conclusion and the observation most likely to falsify it.
